newsitem.title: USA: POLL-US June PPI seen flat, low inflation persists.
newsitem.headline: POLL-US June PPI seen flat, low inflation persists.

text.p: Lower energy prices kept a lid on U.S. wholesale prices in June, contributing to a persistent picture of subdued inflation at the wholesale level, economists said.

In a Reuters poll, economists, on average, forecast that the U.S. Producer Price Index, due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT on Friday, would be flat in June and would be up 0.1 percent without its more volatile food and energy items.
In May PPI fell 0.3 percent both with and without its food and energy components.
Deflation in the energy sector helped restrain wholesale prices, economists said.
"We see energy prices dropping again," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc. "That's the major factor pulling the overall index lower."
Moran forecasts a 0.1-percent drop in overall PPI and a 0.1 percent rise in so-called "core PPI," which excludes food and energy components.
Core PPI ought to be up slightly since "a long list of prices" that declined in May should have stabilized or risen somewhat in June, Moran said.

"Food prices have been down since December," said James Glassman, senior economist at Chase Securities Inc. The unwinding of energy prices from last year's rise to $25 a barrel is also keeping overall PPI from rising, he said.

Another factor contributing to the scenario of lower prices is that import prices have been dropping. This is partly due to the strong dollar and partly due to excess production capacity in the economies of the major U.S. trading partners, particularly in Asia, he said.
"The economies of our trading partners are weak so there's a lot of unusued capacity abroad," said Glassman.
Sam Kahan, president of A.S.K. Financial Research, said energy and food prices seem to have fallen in June.
"A major uncertainty is what happened to automobile prices," said Kahan. "Demand was on the soft side but the seasonal adjustments look for a bit of an increase in prices."

Kahan forecasts a 0.1 percent increase in both overall and core PPI for June. He said such a slight increase would hardly mean that prices had begun to surge. But after months of declines in PPI, another drop would persuade people that producers' ability to raise prices "is very, very weak."
"Producer prices in June were well contained," concurred Marilyn Schaja, money market economist at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp.
Kahan estimates gross domestic product grew at a 2.0 percent annual rate in the quarter ended June 30, and he sees GDP growing at a 2.5-3.0 percent rate in the third quarter.

Given current price stability and a lack of evidence that the economy is growing at a pace that is likely to foster inflation, "the Federal Reserve will sit tight and do nothing" to interest rates, he said.
